llm.paragraph: Without having reviewed the specific papers, a generic expectation based on general familiarity with this research area would be that antioxidant supplementation with vitamin C and/or E most often shows no significant effect on exercise training adaptations, though a meaningful minority of studies report blunted adaptations—particularly for endurance-related molecular signaling (e.g., mitochondrial biogenesis markers) when high-dose antioxidants are given chronically alongside training, especially in previously untrained or moderately trained individuals with high supplementation doses. Enhanced adaptations would be expected to be reported rarely, if at all, and mainly in contexts of pre-existing oxidative stress or micronutrient deficiency. Given the aggregate summary indicating a majority "no effect" finding with moderate agreement (~70%) across a small set of primary studies (11 findings from 5 papers), this is a plausible but low-confidence generic prior; the actual literature could easily diverge from this expectation given the limited number of grounded sources, heterogeneity in dosing, timing, training modality, and outcome measures typically seen in this field, so this summary should be treated as an uncertain, ungrounded baseline rather than a substantive conclusion.
